sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what CI/CD means: how continuous integration, delivery and deployment differ, why teams need automation and what a modern pipeline looks like.

CI/CD is one of the most important ideas in modern software delivery. CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (or Continuous Deployment): the practice of automatically building, testing, and releasing code every time a developer makes a change, so software can go from a commit to production quickly and reliably. If you have ever wondered why some teams release several times a day while others are terrified to deploy once a month, the answer often comes down to whether they have built a strong CI/CD pipeline. In simple terms, CI/CD is the practice of using automation to move code from a developer's commit to a tested, deployable, and sometimes production-ready release.

This tutorial is an in-depth introduction to CI/CD for beginners. By the end, you will understand what CI/CD means, why teams needed it in the first place, how Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment differ, what a pipeline is made of, and why GitLab CI/CD is such a practical place to start.

sections.title: The Problem Before CI/CD
paragraphs: To understand why CI/CD matters, it helps to imagine software development before these practices became common.

A team of developers would each work on features for days or weeks in isolation. One person changed the login page. Another updated the database schema. A third modified the API. A fourth added a background job. Everyone was productive on their own machine, but the real pain started when it was time to combine everything.
This painful moment was often called integration hell.

Integration hell happened when teams delayed merging their changes for too long. Because everyone was working separately, changes drifted apart. One branch depended on an old API contract. Another assumed a package version that had changed. A third introduced a configuration difference that only appeared in staging. When the team finally merged everything together, hidden conflicts exploded at once.
Common symptoms included:
Instead of a smooth flow, software delivery became a stressful event.

Even when the code technically worked, getting it into production was often a manual checklist. Someone would log into a server, pull the latest code, install dependencies, restart services, clear caches, and hope nothing was missed. Maybe a wiki page documented the process. Maybe it did not. Maybe only one experienced engineer knew the right sequence of commands.
Manual deployments created several risks:

The later a bug is found, the more expensive it usually is to fix. If a unit test fails two minutes after a commit, the developer can correct it quickly. If the same bug is discovered three weeks later during release testing, the team must re-create the context, trace multiple changes, and delay the release.
Before CI/CD, teams often found problems too late because they waited too long to integrate, test, and deliver. That delay slowed learning and increased risk.
CI/CD emerged as the answer to this exact set of problems.

sections.title: Key CI/CD Concepts You Should Know
paragraphs: If you are learning what a CI/CD pipeline is, these terms appear everywhere.
A pipeline is the full automated workflow for a change. It contains stages and jobs and produces results like pass, fail, or blocked.
A job is one task performed by the pipeline, such as running tests or deploying an app.
A stage groups related jobs and helps define order, such as build before test and test before deploy.
An artifact is a file produced by a job and passed along or saved for later use. Examples include:

sections.title: Benefits of CI/CD
paragraphs: CI/CD is not just about automation for its own sake. It creates real operational and developer benefits.
When the path from commit to release is automated, teams can ship more often. You do not need a long manual checklist for every deployment. Smaller, more frequent releases become practical.
Because changes are tested continuously, broken code is caught earlier. Automated checks create a quality gate before code reaches users.
Developers work better when they trust the system around them. If every commit is validated automatically, engineers can refactor, improve, and release with much more confidence.
Manual steps often vary depending on who runs them. A pipeline runs the same way every time, which reduces hidden differences between developers, environments, and deployments.

Modern CI/CD platforms record who triggered a pipeline, what commit was built, which jobs passed, and when deployment happened. That history is valuable for debugging, compliance, and incident review.

Because everyone works against the same automated standards, collaboration improves. New team members can understand the delivery process by reading the pipeline configuration instead of learning secret tribal knowledge.

paragraphs: Imagine a small web application team using GitLab.
A developer fixes a bug in the checkout process and pushes the change to a branch. Immediately, a pipeline starts.

First, the build stage installs dependencies and packages the app. Next, the test stage runs unit tests, a few API checks, and a linter. Everything passes. Then the deploy stage publishes the build to a staging environment where teammates can review it.

A product manager confirms the fix works. Because the team uses Continuous Delivery, production deployment is available as a manual approval step. An engineer clicks deploy, and the exact tested artifact goes live.
In a more mature setup using Continuous Deployment, that last click would not be necessary. The same passing pipeline would send the change straight to production automatically.

That is the practical power of CI/CD.

sections.title: The CI/CD Tools Landscape
paragraphs: Many tools can implement CI/CD. The best choice depends on your workflow, hosting model, team size, and platform preferences. Here is a brief beginner comparison of major tools.

GitLab CI/CD is built directly into GitLab. Pipelines are defined in .gitlab-ci.yml, stored in the repository, and executed by runners. It is a strong all-in-one option for teams who want version control, merge requests, and CI/CD in one platform.
GitHub Actions is tightly integrated with GitHub. Workflows live in YAML files under .github/workflows. It is popular for GitHub-centered teams and has a large marketplace of reusable actions.

Jenkins is one of the oldest and most flexible CI/CD tools. It can integrate with almost anything, but it usually requires more setup, plugin management, and maintenance than newer built-in platforms.
CircleCI is a cloud-focused CI/CD tool known for speed and ease of use. It supports configuration as code and integrates with popular version control systems.

Argo CD focuses on GitOps-style Kubernetes deployments rather than general-purpose CI. Teams often pair it with another CI tool. It is especially strong when Git is treated as the source of truth for cluster state.

sections.title: Why GitLab CI/CD Is a Great Choice
paragraphs: If you are learning GitLab CI/CD for beginners, GitLab is a great place to start for several reasons.

On GitLab.com, shared runners often let teams get started without provisioning their own infrastructure. That lowers the barrier to entry.
GitLab makes it easy to see pipeline status, job logs, artifacts, environments, and deployment history in one interface.
You can begin with a tiny pipeline that only echoes a message, then grow into testing, caching, Docker builds, environments, deployments, security scans, and more.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

Continuous integration is about merging work frequently and verifying each change automatically. Every commit triggers a build and a test run, so integration problems surface within minutes instead of at the end of a sprint. Continuous delivery extends that so every change that passes is packaged and provably releasable, with the final push to production left as a human decision. Continuous deployment removes that last manual gate: anything passing the pipeline goes live automatically. The abbreviation CD is genuinely ambiguous and covers the second and third, which is why it is worth being explicit about which one a team means.
Do I need CI/CD for a small project?

The continuous integration half pays for itself almost immediately, even solo. A pipeline that runs your tests on every push takes an hour to set up and catches the class of mistake that is otherwise found by a user. The deployment half is more of a judgement call, if you deploy once a month by hand and it works, automating it can wait. A reasonable order is tests on every commit first, then automated builds, then automated deployment to staging, and production deployment last once you trust the earlier stages.
How long should a CI pipeline take?

Under ten minutes for the feedback developers wait on, and ideally under five. The number matters because it changes behaviour: past roughly fifteen minutes people stop waiting for results, start batching changes, and the fast feedback that justifies CI disappears. When a pipeline grows too slow, the usual wins are running independent jobs in parallel, caching dependencies between runs, and splitting long test suites so only the affected parts run on every commit while the full suite runs on merge.
What is the difference between a pipeline, a stage and a job?

A job is a single unit of work, run the tests, build the image, deploy to staging, executed by a runner in its own environment. A stage is a named group of jobs that run in parallel with each other, such as build, test and deploy. A pipeline is the whole sequence of stages triggered by an event, usually a push or a merge request. Stages run in order and, by default, a stage only begins once every job in the previous one has succeeded.
Which CI/CD tool should I learn?

The concepts transfer almost completely, so the specific tool matters less than people expect. Stages, jobs, runners, artifacts and caching exist in all of them under slightly different names. GitLab CI/CD is a good one to learn first because the whole pipeline is defined in a single .gitlab-ci.yml file in your repository and the platform includes the registry, runners and environments without extra setup. GitHub Actions is the other obvious choice given how much code lives on GitHub. Learning either one well makes picking up the other a matter of hours.
Does CI/CD mean deploying to production automatically?

No, and conflating the two puts a lot of teams off. Continuous integration is only about verifying changes automatically, and it delivers most of the value on its own. Automated deployment to production is a separate decision that depends on your test coverage, your ability to roll back quickly, and your appetite for risk. Plenty of mature teams run excellent CI with a deliberate human approval before production, and that is a perfectly legitimate place to stop.

sections.title: Debugging a Failing Job Step by Step
paragraphs: Sooner or later, your first “real” pipeline will fail. That is normal.
A calm debugging process helps a lot.
Look at the pipeline graph and identify which specific job failed.
Read the log carefully from top to bottom. Search for the first genuine error.
Does the image contain the tool you are calling? For example, npm test needs Node and npm.
If the same command fails locally, the issue may be in the code or scripts rather than GitLab.
Do not change ten things at once. Small, deliberate edits are easier to reason about.
Each new push creates another feedback cycle. That loop is the learning engine of CI/CD.

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: To create your first GitLab CI/CD pipeline, you place a .gitlab-ci.yml file in the repository root, define stages and jobs, choose appropriate images, commit the file, push it, and watch GitLab trigger the pipeline. A runner executes the work, the UI shows the status, and job logs tell you exactly what happened.

Once you are comfortable with this flow, you are ready to learn more advanced topics such as artifacts, caching, variables, rules, environments, and deployment strategies. But the core idea stays simple:
push code, let the pipeline run, read the feedback, improve the system.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Where does the .gitlab-ci.yml file go?

In the root of your repository, on the branch you want it to run for. GitLab detects it automatically on push and starts a pipeline. There is nothing to enable in the UI for a basic setup. The filename and location matter exactly: a file named gitlab-ci.yml without the leading dot, or one placed in a subdirectory, is ignored silently and you will see no pipeline at all rather than an error. The path can be changed in project settings, but the default is what most examples assume.
Why is my pipeline stuck pending?

No runner has picked the job up. The three common causes are that shared runners are disabled for the project, that your job specifies a tags: value no available runner has, and that you are on a self-managed instance with no registered runner at all. Open the job and GitLab usually states which of these it is. Tag mismatches are the most frequent. A job tagged docker only runs on a runner registered with that same tag, and a typo leaves it waiting indefinitely.
What is the difference between shared and self-hosted runners?

Shared runners are provided by GitLab, require no setup, and are billed by the minute on GitLab.com beyond the free allowance. Self-hosted runners are machines you register and operate yourself, which gives you control over the hardware, lets jobs reach private networks, and removes per-minute costs at the price of maintaining them. Most teams start on shared runners and move specific jobs to self-hosted ones when they need more resources, faster builds through warm caches, or access to internal systems.
Why does my job fail with "command not found"?

The job's Docker image does not contain the tool you are calling. Each job runs in a fresh container from the image: you specify, with nothing inherited from other jobs or from your laptop. If a job runs npm ci it needs a Node image; if it runs aws s3 cp it needs the AWS CLI installed. Either choose an image that already includes the tool, or install it in a before_script. Installing tools on every run is slower, so a purpose-built image is usually worth it once a pipeline stabilises.
Do I need a Dockerfile to use GitLab CI/CD?

No. Jobs run inside a container chosen with the image: keyword, and that image can be any public one, node:22, python:3.12, golang:1.23. You only need your own Dockerfile if you are building an image as part of the pipeline, or if you want a custom job environment with your specific toolchain preinstalled. Beginning with an off-the-shelf image is the normal starting point.
How do I see why a job failed?

Open the job in the GitLab UI and read the log from the bottom up. The failing command and its output are almost always in the last twenty lines, above the exit code. Each job log shows the full script as it ran, so you can see exactly which command produced the error. For problems you cannot reproduce from the log, adding set -x at the start of the script prints each command before running it, which makes variable expansion and path problems visible immediately.

gitlab-cicd-getting-started.markdown:
If you want to learn **GitLab CI/CD**, the fastest path is to build a real pipeline yourself. The good news is that GitLab makes the beginner experience surprisingly approachable. You do not need a separate CI server, a complicated plugin system, or a deep background in release engineering. In most cases, you only need a GitLab repository and a single file named `.gitlab-ci.yml`.

This tutorial walks you through **getting started with GitLab CI/CD** from scratch. You will learn what prerequisites you need, where the configuration file lives, how a simple pipeline is structured, what a GitLab Runner does, how jobs are matched to runners, how pipelines get triggered, how to read logs, how to debug common first-time mistakes, and how to build up from an echo-based demo to a more realistic Node.js test pipeline.

## Prerequisites

Before you create your first pipeline, make sure you have a few basics in place.

### 1. A GitLab account

You need access to GitLab, either on GitLab.com or a self-managed GitLab instance. If you are using GitLab.com, many starter projects can use shared runners immediately.

### 2. A repository

You need a project repository where the pipeline configuration file will live. This can be:

- a brand-new test repository
- an existing application repository
- a simple demo repo with a README and one source file

### 3. Permission to run pipelines

In most personal or team projects, if you can push to the repository, you can trigger pipelines. In some organizations, runner access or protected branch rules may affect what can run.

### 4. Basic Git workflow knowledge

You should know how to:

- create or edit files locally
- commit changes
- push to GitLab
- open the project in the GitLab web UI

That is enough to begin.

## What Is `.gitlab-ci.yml`?

The heart of GitLab CI/CD is a file named **`.gitlab-ci.yml`**.

This file is the pipeline definition. It tells GitLab:

- what stages exist
- what jobs should run
- what commands each job executes
- which Docker image to use
- when jobs should run
- what artifacts, rules, or variables apply

### Where the file goes

`.gitlab-ci.yml` must be placed in the **root of the repository**.

That means its path should look like this:

```text
my-project/
  .gitlab-ci.yml
  README.md
  src/
  package.json
```

If you accidentally place the file inside a subdirectory such as `ci/.gitlab-ci.yml` without using advanced include patterns, GitLab will not treat it as the main pipeline definition for the project.

### Why the file matters

GitLab reads `.gitlab-ci.yml` whenever a pipeline event occurs. Because the file lives in version control, your pipeline is managed as code. That means you can review changes, compare versions, and evolve the delivery process alongside the application.

## Your First `.gitlab-ci.yml`: A Minimal 3-Stage Pipeline

A great beginner exercise is a simple pipeline that does not depend on a real application yet. It just shows the structure of a GitLab pipeline.

Create `.gitlab-ci.yml` in the repository root with the following content:

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-job:
  stage: build
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - echo "Building the application"
    - echo "Pretend a build happens here"

test-job:
  stage: test
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - echo "Running tests"
    - echo "Pretend automated tests run here"

deploy-job:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - echo "Deploying the application"
    - echo "Pretend a deployment happens here"
```

This is not a production pipeline, but it is a complete working example of a **3-stage GitLab pipeline**.

### What this first pipeline teaches you

It shows you the core building blocks:

- a pipeline can have multiple stages
- each stage can have one or more jobs
- jobs execute shell commands from `script`
- GitLab shows the result of each job in the UI
- stages normally run in the listed order

Once this file is committed and pushed, GitLab should create a pipeline automatically.

## Breaking Down Each Part of the YAML

YAML is indentation-sensitive, so learning the structure matters.

### `stages`

The `stages` array defines the order of major pipeline phases.

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy
```

In this example, GitLab will try to run all build-stage jobs first. If that stage succeeds, it will move to the test stage. If test succeeds, it will move to deploy.

Think of stages as signposts that organize the journey.

### Job names

The names `build-job`, `test-job`, and `deploy-job` are job identifiers.

```yaml
build-job:
```

A job name can be almost anything descriptive. Good names help you and your teammates quickly understand what each job does.

For example:

- `install-dependencies`
- `run-unit-tests`
- `deploy-staging`

### `stage`

The `stage` keyword assigns a job to one of the declared stages.

```yaml
stage: test
```

If the stage name is misspelled or does not exist in the `stages` list, the pipeline will fail to validate or behave unexpectedly.

### `script`

The `script` section is the actual list of commands that the runner executes.

```yaml
script:
  - echo "Running tests"
  - echo "Pretend automated tests run here"
```

If any command in the script exits with a non-zero status, the job usually fails.

### `image`

The `image` keyword tells GitLab which container image to use for the job runtime.

```yaml
image: alpine:3.20
```

For a beginner demo, Alpine is a convenient lightweight Linux image. In real projects, you often choose images that already contain the tools you need, such as:

- `node:20`
- `python:3.12`
- `golang:1.24`
- `maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21`

## Why GitLab Uses Runners

A pipeline definition lives in GitLab, but GitLab itself does not magically execute your shell commands. That is the job of a **GitLab Runner**.

A **runner** is an agent that picks up CI/CD jobs and runs them in an execution environment.

### What a runner actually does

When a pipeline starts, GitLab looks for an available runner that is allowed to execute the job. The runner then:

1. fetches the job definition
2. prepares the environment
3. checks out the repository code
4. runs the script commands
5. streams logs back to GitLab
6. reports success or failure

Without a runner, the pipeline definition exists, but nothing can actually run.

## Shared Runners vs Self-Hosted Runners

When learning **GitLab Runner basics**, you will encounter two common models.

### Shared runners

**Shared runners** are provided for multiple projects, usually managed centrally by GitLab.com or by your organization. They are the easiest option for beginners because you often do not need to install anything yourself.

Benefits of shared runners:

- fast setup
- no infrastructure to manage
- good for standard builds and tests
- ideal for learning and small projects

Possible limits:

- usage quotas on some plans
- less control over the environment
- not suitable for private internal network access

### Self-hosted runners

**Self-hosted runners** are runners you install and manage yourself. They are useful when you need:

- access to private infrastructure
- custom tools or hardware
- tighter performance control
- specialized security or compliance boundaries

They require more maintenance, but they offer more flexibility.

## How GitLab Matches a Job to a Runner

A beginner question often sounds like this: **How does GitLab decide where a job runs?**

GitLab uses runner availability, scope, and optionally **tags**.

### Shared pool matching

If your project is allowed to use shared runners and a job has no special tag requirement, GitLab can send that job to the shared runner pool.

### Tagged runner matching

Runners can be registered with tags such as:

- `docker`
- `node`
- `linux`
- `production`

A job can request matching tags:

```yaml
test-node:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  tags:
    - docker
    - node
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test
```

GitLab will look for a runner that has all required tags. If none are available, the job will stay pending.

### Why tags matter

Tags help make sure the right job lands on the right infrastructure. For example, a deployment job that needs VPN access or cloud credentials should not run on an arbitrary general-purpose runner.

## Triggering a Pipeline

There are several ways to start a pipeline in GitLab.

### On push

The most common trigger is a Git push. If `.gitlab-ci.yml` exists and the branch is configured normally, a pipeline is created after the push.

### On merge request

Pipelines can also run when a merge request is opened or updated. These are especially valuable because they show whether a proposed change passes validation before it is merged.

### Manually

You can trigger a pipeline manually from the GitLab UI. This is useful for reruns, ad hoc checks, or deployment jobs that should only run on demand.

### On schedule

GitLab can run pipelines on a schedule, such as every night or every Monday morning. Scheduled pipelines are useful for routine maintenance tasks, dependency scans, or regular integration checks.

### Why multiple triggers are helpful

Different triggers support different workflows:

- push pipelines give fast developer feedback
- merge request pipelines protect code review quality
- manual pipelines support controlled release actions
- scheduled pipelines catch issues over time

## Pushing Your First Pipeline

Once your `.gitlab-ci.yml` file exists, commit and push it.

A typical local flow looks like this:

```bash
git add .gitlab-ci.yml
git commit -m "Add first GitLab CI pipeline"
git push origin main
```

After the push, open the project in GitLab and navigate to the pipeline view.

## Watching the Pipeline Run in the GitLab UI

GitLab provides a visual pipeline interface that is beginner-friendly once you know what to look for.

### Pipeline list view

In the **Build > Pipelines** area, you can usually see:

- pipeline ID
- branch or commit reference
- status icon
- author
- start time
- duration

This is the top-level view of what happened.

### Pipeline graph view

Click into a pipeline to see the stage-by-stage layout. This view helps you understand which jobs ran in which order and where a failure happened.

### Job details and logs

Click a job name to open its live or completed log output. This is where you see the commands that ran and the exact output they produced.

### Green, red, and other statuses

The status colors communicate quickly:

- **green** usually means success
- **red** means failure
- **yellow or orange** often indicates running or warning-like states
- **gray** may indicate skipped, pending, or manual states depending on the context

Reading these statuses becomes second nature once you use pipelines regularly.

## Reading Job Logs

Job logs are one of the most important beginner skills in GitLab CI/CD.

### What the output usually includes

A job log often shows:

- runner preparation steps
- repository checkout
- commands from the `script` section
- command output
- any error messages
- final job status

For example, if your script says:

```yaml
script:
  - npm ci
  - npm test
```

then the job log will show the output from both commands.

### How to think about a failing log

When a job fails, ask these questions:

1. Which command failed?
2. Did the environment have the tools it needed?
3. Did a file or dependency go missing?
4. Was the YAML correct but the script logic wrong?
5. Did the job run on the expected branch or runner?

The first meaningful error message is often more useful than the final one. Beginners sometimes scroll straight to the bottom, but the root cause is often earlier in the output.

## Common First-Time Mistakes

Almost everyone hits a few small issues while creating a first pipeline.

### Wrong YAML indentation

YAML uses spaces to define structure. A misplaced indent can break the file.

For example, this is wrong:

```yaml
build-job:
stage: build
  script:
    - echo "Oops"
```

The keys must be indented correctly under the job name.

### Wrong stage name

If a job says `stage: tests` but the `stages` list only contains `test`, GitLab cannot place the job correctly.

### Forgetting to push `.gitlab-ci.yml`

Creating the file locally is not enough. GitLab only sees it after you commit and push it.

### Using the wrong image

If your job runs `npm test` but the image is `alpine:3.20`, npm may not be available unless you install it manually. Pick an image that already contains the tools you need.

### Assuming every project has a runner

If no suitable runner is available, the job may remain pending forever. Check whether shared runners are enabled or whether your project requires a specific tagged runner.

### Editing the file in the wrong location

Remember that the main pipeline file belongs in the root of the repository.

## Building Up to a Real Pipeline: Add a Node.js Test Job

Once the echo-based demo makes sense, the next step is to run something real.

Imagine a Node.js project with a `package.json` and a test script. A basic test pipeline might look like this:

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

test-app:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

deploy-preview:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - echo "Deploy step placeholder"
```

This example introduces a practical improvement: the build and test jobs now run in `node:20`, which already includes Node.js and npm.

### Why `npm ci` is often preferred

In CI, `npm ci` is usually better than `npm install` because it uses the lock file predictably and is designed for automated environments.

### Why the deploy step is still a placeholder

When you are learning, it is smart to separate pipeline structure from deployment complexity. First get the pipeline green. Then add real deployment logic later.

## A Complete Working `.gitlab-ci.yml` Example with Annotations

Here is a beginner-friendly working example that combines the key ideas from this tutorial:

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:20
  script:
    - echo "Installing dependencies"
    - npm ci
    - echo "Building application"
    - npm run build

run-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - echo "Installing dependencies for tests"
    - npm ci
    - echo "Running test suite"
    - npm test

deploy-demo:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - echo "This is where a real deployment command would run"
```

### How to read this file

- `stages` declares the order: build, then test, then deploy.
- `build-app` compiles the project.
- `run-tests` validates it.
- `deploy-demo` stands in for a later real deployment.
- Each job defines its own runtime image.
- Every script section contains the shell commands to execute.

This is still small, but it looks and feels like a real pipeline rather than a toy example.

## The Pipeline Status Badge in Your README

One nice beginner feature in GitLab is the **pipeline status badge**.

A badge is a small status image you can place in your `README.md` to show whether the default branch pipeline is passing.

Why it is useful:

- teammates instantly see project health
- reviewers can quickly check whether the main branch is green
- open source visitors get immediate signal about repository maintenance

The exact badge URL comes from the GitLab UI, but conceptually it turns the pipeline result into a visible quality indicator right on the project homepage.

## Debugging a Failing Job Step by Step

Sooner or later, your first ârealâ pipeline will fail. That is normal.

A calm debugging process helps a lot.

### Step 1: Confirm the failing job

Look at the pipeline graph and identify which specific job failed.

### Step 2: Open the job log

Read the log carefully from top to bottom. Search for the first genuine error.

### Step 3: Check the runtime image

Does the image contain the tool you are calling? For example, `npm test` needs Node and npm.

### Step 4: Compare the command locally

If the same command fails locally, the issue may be in the code or scripts rather than GitLab.

### Step 5: Fix one thing at a time

Do not change ten things at once. Small, deliberate edits are easier to reason about.

### Step 6: Push again and observe

Each new push creates another feedback cycle. That loop is the learning engine of CI/CD.

## Best Beginner Mindset for GitLab CI/CD

When you are just starting, remember these principles:

- start small
- get a green pipeline first
- prefer clear job names
- use the right runtime image
- read logs carefully
- treat `.gitlab-ci.yml` like application code
- evolve the pipeline step by step

The goal is not to build the perfect enterprise pipeline on day one. The goal is to understand the mechanics and create a reliable foundation.

## Final Takeaway

To create your first **GitLab CI/CD pipeline**, you place a `.gitlab-ci.yml` file in the repository root, define stages and jobs, choose appropriate images, commit the file, push it, and watch GitLab trigger the pipeline. A runner executes the work, the UI shows the status, and job logs tell you exactly what happened.

Once you are comfortable with this flow, you are ready to learn more advanced topics such as artifacts, caching, variables, rules, environments, and deployment strategies. But the core idea stays simple:

**push code, let the pipeline run, read the feedback, improve the system.**

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Where does the `.gitlab-ci.yml` file go?**

In the root of your repository, on the branch you want it to run for. GitLab detects it automatically on push and starts a pipeline. There is nothing to enable in the UI for a basic setup. The filename and location matter exactly: a file named `gitlab-ci.yml` without the leading dot, or one placed in a subdirectory, is ignored silently and you will see no pipeline at all rather than an error. The path can be changed in project settings, but the default is what most examples assume.

**Why is my pipeline stuck pending?**

No runner has picked the job up. The three common causes are that shared runners are disabled for the project, that your job specifies a `tags:` value no available runner has, and that you are on a self-managed instance with no registered runner at all. Open the job and GitLab usually states which of these it is. Tag mismatches are the most frequent. A job tagged `docker` only runs on a runner registered with that same tag, and a typo leaves it waiting indefinitely.

**What is the difference between shared and self-hosted runners?**

Shared runners are provided by GitLab, require no setup, and are billed by the minute on GitLab.com beyond the free allowance. Self-hosted runners are machines you register and operate yourself, which gives you control over the hardware, lets jobs reach private networks, and removes per-minute costs at the price of maintaining them. Most teams start on shared runners and move specific jobs to self-hosted ones when they need more resources, faster builds through warm caches, or access to internal systems.

**Why does my job fail with "command not found"?**

The job's Docker image does not contain the tool you are calling. Each job runs in a fresh container from the `image:` you specify, with nothing inherited from other jobs or from your laptop. If a job runs `npm ci` it needs a Node image; if it runs `aws s3 cp` it needs the AWS CLI installed. Either choose an image that already includes the tool, or install it in a `before_script`. Installing tools on every run is slower, so a purpose-built image is usually worth it once a pipeline stabilises.

**Do I need a Dockerfile to use GitLab CI/CD?**

No. Jobs run inside a container chosen with the `image:` keyword, and that image can be any public one, `node:22`, `python:3.12`, `golang:1.23`. You only need your own Dockerfile if you are building an image as part of the pipeline, or if you want a custom job environment with your specific toolchain preinstalled. Beginning with an off-the-shelf image is the normal starting point.

**How do I see why a job failed?**

Open the job in the GitLab UI and read the log from the bottom up. The failing command and its output are almost always in the last twenty lines, above the exit code. Each job log shows the full script as it ran, so you can see exactly which command produced the error. For problems you cannot reproduce from the log, adding `set -x` at the start of the script prints each command before running it, which makes variable expansion and path problems visible immediately.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a pipeline, a stage and a job?

A job is a single unit of work with its own script, running in its own isolated environment on a runner. A stage is a named group of jobs that execute in parallel with each other. A pipeline is one complete run of all the stages, triggered by an event such as a push, a merge request, a tag or a schedule. Stages run in sequence and, by default, each waits for every job in the previous stage to succeed before starting.
Do jobs in the same stage run at the same time?

Yes, provided runners are available to take them. That is the defining property of a stage. Putting two jobs in test means they run concurrently, and the stage is complete only when both finish. If jobs in a stage appear to run one after another, you have fewer free runners than jobs, or the runner's concurrent setting limits how many it will execute simultaneously.
What is the difference between artifacts and cache?

Artifacts preserve a job's output and are guaranteed to reach the jobs that need them, as well as being downloadable from the GitLab UI. Cache stores reusable inputs such as node_modules to make later runs faster, with no guarantee it will be there. It can be missing on a new branch, stale, or absent because the job ran on a different runner. The test is whether the pipeline would still be correct if the data vanished: if yes, cache; if no, artifacts.
Why are two pipelines created every time I push?

Because both branch pipelines and merge request pipelines are running for the same commit. When a branch has an open merge request, GitLab creates a pipeline for the branch and another for the merge request unless you tell it otherwise. The standard fix is a top-level workflow: rules: block that runs the merge request pipeline when one exists, suppresses the branch pipeline in that case, and always runs on the default branch. Defining it once at the top applies it to the whole pipeline.
Why doesn't my rule match on merge requests?

Because $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH is not set in a merge request pipeline. It only exists in branch pipelines, so a condition written against it silently never matches when the pipeline was triggered by a merge request event. Use $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME for the branch name in that context, or branch on $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" to distinguish the pipeline type explicitly.
Can a job start before the previous stage finishes?

Yes, with needs:. Listing the specific jobs a job depends on lets it begin as soon as those have completed, ignoring stage boundaries and turning the pipeline into a directed acyclic graph. This can cut total runtime substantially when job durations are uneven. A deploy that only needs the build no longer waits for a slow test suite. The cost is that the pipeline becomes harder to read, so it is worth using where the time saving is genuine rather than applying it everywhere.

# GitLab CI/CD Pipeline Structure

This page is about the **shape** of a GitLab pipeline. What the moving parts are, how they relate, and where each concept belongs. It is the map. The linked guides are the territory.

If you want the full syntax for defining stages and writing jobs, go straight to [GitLab CI Stages and Jobs](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-stages-jobs).

## Four layers

Everything in GitLab CI/CD sits in one of four layers, and most confusion comes from mixing them up.

| Layer | What it is | Where it is defined |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipeline** | One end-to-end run, triggered by an event | Created by GitLab from `.gitlab-ci.yml` |
| **Stage** | A named group of jobs that run together | `stages:` list |
| **Job** | One unit of work with a script | A top-level key in `.gitlab-ci.yml` |
| **Runner** | The machine or container that executes a job | Registered separately, outside the file |

Read downward: a push creates a **pipeline**, the pipeline contains **stages** in order, each stage contains **jobs** that run in parallel, and each job is handed to a **runner** that actually runs the script.

The layer people forget is the runner. GitLab itself never executes anything. It decides what should run and hands it off. That is why a pipeline with no available runner sits pending forever with no error: nothing is wrong with your configuration, there is simply nobody to do the work.

## The default flow

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-app:
  stage: build
  script: npm run build

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script: npm test

lint:
  stage: test
  script: npm run lint

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh staging
```

That pipeline runs in three waves:

1. `build-app` runs alone.
2. `unit-tests` and `lint` run **at the same time**, because they share a stage.
3. `deploy-staging` runs.

Two rules produce that behaviour, and they are worth stating explicitly because everything else builds on them:

- **Jobs in the same stage run in parallel.**
- **A stage does not start until every job in the previous stage has succeeded.**

A job with no `stage:` key goes into `test` by default, which regularly puts jobs somewhere their author did not intend.

## Breaking the stage lockstep

Strict stage ordering is simple but wasteful. If `lint` takes 20 seconds and `unit-tests` takes 8 minutes, the deploy waits 8 minutes even though it only really depends on the build.

`needs:` replaces stage ordering with explicit dependencies, turning the pipeline into a directed acyclic graph:

```yaml
deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  needs: [build-app]        # start as soon as the build is done
  script: ./deploy.sh staging
```

The job now starts the moment `build-app` finishes, regardless of whether the test stage is still running. On pipelines with uneven job durations this is often the single largest speed-up available.

The trade-off is legibility, a DAG is harder to reason about than a column of stages, so it is worth applying where the saving is real rather than everywhere.

## Where artifacts and cache fit

Every job runs in a **fresh, isolated environment**. Nothing carries over between jobs by default: not files, not installed packages, not environment variables set with `export`. That isolation is what makes pipelines reproducible, and it is also why two separate mechanisms exist for moving data between jobs.

| | Artifacts | Cache |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Preserve job **output** | Reuse job **input** |
| Guaranteed present | Yes | No |
| Visible in the UI | Yes, downloadable | No |
| Scope | Within a pipeline, and afterwards | Across pipelines |
| Typical contents | Build output, test reports, deploy bundles | `node_modules`, pip cache, Maven repository |

The distinction that actually matters is **correctness versus speed**.

Artifacts are a guarantee. A job that declares an artifact will have it available to the jobs that need it, and you can download it weeks later from the pipeline page.

Cache is an optimisation with no guarantee. It may be missing on a new branch, stale from an older run, or absent because the job landed on a different runner. A pipeline must still produce a correct result with every cache empty, if it does not, something that should be an artifact is being treated as cache.

The practical test: **would the pipeline still be correct if this data vanished?** If yes, cache. If no, artifact.

Full detail in [Artifacts](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-artifacts) and [Cache](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-cache).

## What triggers a pipeline

Not all pipelines are the same kind, and several CI variables behave differently depending on which one is running. The most common source of rules that mysteriously never match.

| Type | Triggered by | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Branch pipeline | A push to a branch | `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is set |
| Merge request pipeline | Opening or updating a merge request | `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is **not** set |
| Scheduled pipeline | A cron schedule in the UI | Good for nightly integration suites |
| Tag pipeline | Pushing a tag | The usual release trigger |
| Child pipeline | A `trigger:` job in the same project | Splits large configurations |
| Multi-project pipeline | A `trigger:` job naming another project | Coordinates across repositories |

A rule written as `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"` will never match inside a merge request pipeline, because that variable is not populated there. This catches almost everyone once.

## Controlling the pipeline as a whole

Individual jobs are filtered with `rules:`. The pipeline itself is governed by a top-level `workflow:` block:

```yaml
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH
```

That block is worth understanding because it solves the most common annoyance in GitLab CI: **duplicate pipelines**. Without it, a push to a branch with an open merge request creates both a branch pipeline and a merge request pipeline, doubling your runner minutes and cluttering the UI. The third rule suppresses the branch pipeline when a merge request already exists.

Defining this once at the top is much better than repeating the same conditions on every job.

## Final Takeaway

A GitLab pipeline is four layers: an event creates a **pipeline**, which contains ordered **stages**, which contain parallel **jobs**, each executed by a **runner**. Jobs are isolated from one another, so **artifacts** move guaranteed output forward and **cache** speeds up repeated inputs without any guarantee. `workflow:` decides whether a pipeline runs at all; `rules:` decides which jobs are in it; `needs:` lets you escape strict stage ordering when it costs too much time.

Get those relationships straight and the syntax in the detailed guides is mostly bookkeeping.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a pipeline, a stage and a job?**

A job is a single unit of work with its own script, running in its own isolated environment on a runner. A stage is a named group of jobs that execute in parallel with each other. A pipeline is one complete run of all the stages, triggered by an event such as a push, a merge request, a tag or a schedule. Stages run in sequence and, by default, each waits for every job in the previous stage to succeed before starting.

**Do jobs in the same stage run at the same time?**

Yes, provided runners are available to take them. That is the defining property of a stage. Putting two jobs in `test` means they run concurrently, and the stage is complete only when both finish. If jobs in a stage appear to run one after another, you have fewer free runners than jobs, or the runner's `concurrent` setting limits how many it will execute simultaneously.

**What is the difference between artifacts and cache?**

Artifacts preserve a job's output and are guaranteed to reach the jobs that need them, as well as being downloadable from the GitLab UI. Cache stores reusable inputs such as `node_modules` to make later runs faster, with no guarantee it will be there. It can be missing on a new branch, stale, or absent because the job ran on a different runner. The test is whether the pipeline would still be correct if the data vanished: if yes, cache; if no, artifacts.

**Why are two pipelines created every time I push?**

Because both branch pipelines and merge request pipelines are running for the same commit. When a branch has an open merge request, GitLab creates a pipeline for the branch and another for the merge request unless you tell it otherwise. The standard fix is a top-level `workflow: rules:` block that runs the merge request pipeline when one exists, suppresses the branch pipeline in that case, and always runs on the default branch. Defining it once at the top applies it to the whole pipeline.

**Why doesn't my rule match on merge requests?**

Because `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is not set in a merge request pipeline. It only exists in branch pipelines, so a condition written against it silently never matches when the pipeline was triggered by a merge request event. Use `$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME` for the branch name in that context, or branch on `$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"` to distinguish the pipeline type explicitly.

**Can a job start before the previous stage finishes?**

Yes, with `needs:`. Listing the specific jobs a job depends on lets it begin as soon as those have completed, ignoring stage boundaries and turning the pipeline into a directed acyclic graph. This can cut total runtime substantially when job durations are uneven. A deploy that only needs the build no longer waits for a slow test suite. The cost is that the pipeline becomes harder to read, so it is worth using where the time saving is genuine rather than applying it everywhere.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Define GitLab CI stages and jobs: the stages keyword and ordering, job scripts, core job keywords, rules and only/except conditions, and parallel jobs.

GitLab CI/CD pipelines look simple at first: you commit a .gitlab-ci.yml file, GitLab reads it, and a runner executes the jobs. The real power comes from how you break that work into stages and jobs. If you understand those two building blocks well, you can design pipelines that are readable, fast, and safe.

This lesson explains how stages set the high-level order of a pipeline, how jobs do the actual work, how to control when jobs run, and how to speed things up with parallel execution and DAG-style dependencies.

sections.title: What Are Stages in GitLab CI?
paragraphs: A stage is a named phase in your pipeline. Think of stages as checkpoints in a delivery process. A common sequence is:
Stages create a clean mental model. Instead of seeing a long flat list of jobs, you see a workflow: build the application, verify it, then release it.
GitLab executes stages sequentially by default. Every job in one stage must finish successfully before the next stage starts. That behavior is useful because it creates natural safety gates.
For example, you usually do not want deployment to begin if tests are still failing. With stages, GitLab gives you that protection automatically.
GitLab CI/CD Pipeline Stages (Sequential)
Each stage must pass before the next begins. Jobs within a stage can run in parallel
Inside a stage, however, multiple jobs can run at the same time if runners are available. That means the stage order is sequential, but the jobs within a stage can be parallel.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

sections.title: Default Stages in GitLab
paragraphs: If you do not define a custom stages: array, GitLab has default stage names. The most commonly discussed defaults are:

In practice, most real projects define their own explicit stages: list even when they use those same names. Doing so makes the pipeline easier to read and prevents confusion later when you add extra phases such as lint, package, security, or release.
A beginner-friendly pipeline might look like this:
A more realistic production pipeline might look like:
The names are flexible. GitLab does not care what you call a stage as long as jobs refer to valid stage names.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

sections.title: The stages: Keyword and Ordering Rules
paragraphs: The stages: keyword defines the order of stages from top to bottom.

GitLab uses the list order exactly as written. If a job belongs to integration_test, it will not start until every required job in unit_test is done. If a stage name is missing from stages:, the job configuration is invalid.
A few practical rules matter:
That last point is one of the biggest reasons stages are useful. They turn your pipeline into a guarded path rather than a pile of unrelated tasks.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - lint
  - unit_test
  - integration_test
  - deploy_staging
  - deploy_production

sections.title: What Are Jobs?
paragraphs: A job is the actual unit of execution in GitLab CI/CD. It is a named block in .gitlab-ci.yml that tells a runner what to do.
Here, build-app is the job name. It belongs to the build stage, runs in a node:20 container, and executes the shell commands listed under script:.
You can think of a job as a task card with three basic questions:
A pipeline can have one job or many. In a real project, you usually separate concerns into small focused jobs because that makes failures easier to debug.

codeBlock.code:
build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

sections.title: Core Job Keywords
paragraphs: Jobs support many keywords, but a few appear in almost every pipeline.
script is the heart of the job. It contains the commands the runner executes.
If any command exits with a non-zero status, the job fails.
before_script defines commands that run before script. It is commonly used for setup steps such as printing tool versions or preparing environment files.
You can define before_script globally or per job.
after_script runs after the main script, even if the job fails. It is useful for cleanup, diagnostics, or collecting logs.
image chooses the container image used by the job when you run on Docker-based runners.
This lets different jobs use different runtimes in the same pipeline. Your frontend build can use Node, a test job can use Python, and a packaging job can use Alpine.
tags tell GitLab which runners are allowed to pick up the job. This matters when you have multiple self-hosted runners with different capabilities.
If no available runner matches the tags, the job stays pending.
environment connects a job to a deployment environment such as staging or production.
This makes deployments visible in GitLab and is especially useful once you start promoting releases between environments.

codeBlock.code:
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

sections.title: A Simple Multi-Stage Pipeline
paragraphs: Let us combine stages and jobs in one example:
That single behavior explains a huge part of how GitLab pipelines feel in practice.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

lint:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run lint

deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - echo "Deploying application"

sections.title: Controlling When Jobs Run with rules
paragraphs: Not every job should run on every pipeline. You might want to run lightweight checks on feature branches, but deploy only from main. Modern GitLab pipelines usually use rules for this.
A rule can inspect branch names, pipeline sources, file changes, and desired timing.
Use if expressions to decide based on CI variables.
That job only runs on the main branch.
You can also target merge request pipelines:
Use changes to run a job only when specific files are touched.
This is powerful for monorepos and large projects because it avoids unnecessary work.
A rule can also set when the job runs.
Common when values include:
GitLab evaluates rules from top to bottom and stops at the first match. That means ordering is important.
On main, the first rule matches and the job becomes manual. GitLab does not continue to later rules.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: only and except: Older Syntax
paragraphs: Before rules became the preferred approach, GitLab pipelines often used only and except.

only and except still appear in older repositories and are worth understanding, but rules are more flexible and usually easier to extend. For new pipelines, prefer rules unless you are maintaining an existing style for consistency.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh
  only:
    - main

sections.title: Manual Jobs with when: manual
paragraphs: Some steps should not run automatically, even in a successful pipeline. Production deploys are the classic example. GitLab supports this with manual jobs.
When the pipeline reaches this job, GitLab pauses and shows a play button in the UI. A human can then trigger the deployment when ready.
Manual jobs are useful for:
They are one of the simplest ways to add a control gate without redesigning the entire pipeline.

codeBlock.code:
deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy-production.sh
  when: manual
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: Parallel Jobs
paragraphs: Parallelism is where GitLab can save you a lot of time.
The easiest form of parallelism comes automatically. If you place multiple jobs in the same stage, GitLab can run them at the same time.
If you have enough runners, those three jobs can execute together.
GitLab also lets you split one job into several copies.
GitLab creates four parallel job instances. This is useful when your test suite can be sharded across workers.
For structured combinations, use parallel:matrix.
That single job definition expands into multiple jobs:
Matrix builds are excellent for cross-version testing and multi-environment packaging.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - test

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm test

lint:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm run lint

security-audit:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm audit --production

sections.title: Job Dependencies with needs for DAG Pipelines
paragraphs: Stages are easy to understand, but sometimes they are too strict. Suppose one test job only depends on the build output, not on every other test job. With normal stage ordering, it still waits for the full previous stage.
The needs keyword solves this by creating a DAG pipeline.
With needs, unit-tests can start as soon as build-app finishes, even if other jobs in the earlier stage are still running or if the stage structure would otherwise cause waiting.
This produces a directed acyclic graph, or DAG, instead of a strict stage-by-stage wall.
A common pattern is to keep stages for readability but use needs to remove unnecessary waiting.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-app:
  stage: build
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  needs:
    - build-app
  script:
    - npm test

lint:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm run lint

sections.title: Complete Realistic .gitlab-ci.yml Example for a Node.js App
paragraphs: The following example brings the concepts together. It assumes a Node.js application with linting, unit tests, a build step, and a manual production deploy.
This is the kind of pipeline structure you see in real teams: clear phases, controlled execution, and faster paths where dependencies allow it.

codeBlock.code:
stages:
  - validate
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

default:
  image: node:20
  before_script:
    - node --version
    - npm --version

lint:
  stage: validate
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run lint
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH'

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test -- --ci
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH'

build-app:
  stage: build
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH'

package-app:
  stage: test
  needs:
    - build-app
  script:
    - test -d dist
    - tar -czf app.tar.gz dist
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH'

integration-tests:
  stage: test
  needs:
    - build-app
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run test:integration
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      when: on_success

preview-deploy:
  stage: deploy
  environment:
    name: preview/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: https://$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.preview.example.com
  script:
    - ./scripts/deploy-preview.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'

production-deploy:
  stage: deploy
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://example.com
  script:
    - ./scripts/deploy-production.sh
  when: manual
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

sections.title: Practical Tips for Better Jobs and Stages
paragraphs: A few habits make pipelines much easier to maintain:
Names like test or build are acceptable in tiny demos, but in real repositories clearer names help:
A giant job is hard to debug. If linting fails, you should not need to scroll through packaging logs to find the issue. Smaller jobs also enable better parallelism.
Do not let every expensive job run on every branch by default. Ask whether it belongs on feature branches, merge requests, scheduled pipelines, tags, or only on main.
If the pipeline graph becomes hard to understand, simplify it. Fast pipelines are good, but readable pipelines are maintainable.
Use a Node image for Node work, a Python image for Python work, and a lightweight utility image for simple shell tasks. This keeps jobs predictable.

sections.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
paragraphs: Forgetting to declare a stage A job references stage: package, but package is missing from stages:.
Putting every command in one job This removes the advantages of visibility and parallel execution.
Using only and except everywhere in new pipelines It works, but new work is usually cleaner with rules.
Making production deployment automatic too early A manual gate is often safer while your pipeline matures.
Ignoring runner tags A job can stay pending forever if no runner matches its required tags.

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: Stages give your pipeline structure. Jobs do the work. rules decide when work should happen. parallel and needs make the pipeline faster. Once those concepts click, .gitlab-ci.yml stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like a workflow you control.
The next step after mastering stages and jobs is learning how files move through the pipeline with artifacts and how repeated work is sped up with cache.

sections.title: Knowledge Check
paragraphs: What is the default behavior of GitLab when you define stages named build, test, and deploy?
Why is rules usually preferred over only and except in newer GitLab pipelines?
What is the main benefit of using needs in a GitLab pipeline?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a stage and a job in GitLab CI?

A job is a single unit of work with its own script, its own container and its own runner. A stage is a named group of jobs. Jobs within the same stage run in parallel with one another, and by default a stage does not begin until every job in the previous stage has succeeded. So stages: [build, test, deploy] means all build jobs finish before any test job starts. The needs: keyword breaks that lockstep when you want a job to start as soon as its own dependency is ready.
What is the difference between rules, only and except?

only and except are the older syntax and are no longer recommended, though they still work. rules: replaced them and is considerably more capable: it evaluates conditions in order, stops at the first match, and can set when, allow_failure and variables per rule. A practical difference that catches people is that rules and only/except cannot be used in the same job. GitLab rejects the pipeline. New pipelines should use rules exclusively.
Why do my jobs run in the wrong order?

Almost always a stage that is not declared in the stages: list, or jobs assigned to stages in an order different from the one you expect. Job execution order comes entirely from stage order, not from the order jobs appear in the file. A job with no stage: key is placed in test by default, which frequently puts it earlier or later than intended. If you want ordering based on actual data dependencies rather than stages, use needs: to build a directed acyclic graph.
What does needs: do and when should I use it?

needs: lets a job start as soon as the specific jobs it names have finished, instead of waiting for the whole previous stage. That turns a strictly sequential pipeline into a DAG and can cut total runtime substantially when some branches are much slower than others. It also implicitly fetches artifacts from the jobs it names. The trade-off is that the pipeline graph becomes harder to reason about, so it is worth applying where the time saving is real rather than everywhere by default.
How do I make a job manual?

Set when: manual on the job, which adds a play button in the pipeline view and leaves the job waiting until someone clicks it. This is the standard way to gate a production deployment behind human approval. By default a manual job is optional and the pipeline can succeed without it; adding allow_failure: false makes the pipeline block until it is run, which is what you want when the manual step is genuinely required rather than a convenience.
Why is my job not running at all?

Either a rules, only or except condition excluded it, or it is waiting for a runner. Open the pipeline and check whether the job appears at all. A job filtered out by rules is absent from the pipeline entirely, while a job waiting for a runner shows as pending. For rules problems, the usual cause is a branch or pipeline-source condition that does not match: a rule written for $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main" never fires on a merge request pipeline, where the branch variable is not set and $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME applies instead.

gitlab-ci-stages-jobs.markdown:
# GitLab CI/CD Pipeline Structure

This page is about the **shape** of a GitLab pipeline. What the moving parts are, how they relate, and where each concept belongs. It is the map. The linked guides are the territory.

If you want the full syntax for defining stages and writing jobs, go straight to [GitLab CI Stages and Jobs](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-stages-jobs).

## Four layers

Everything in GitLab CI/CD sits in one of four layers, and most confusion comes from mixing them up.

| Layer | What it is | Where it is defined |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipeline** | One end-to-end run, triggered by an event | Created by GitLab from `.gitlab-ci.yml` |
| **Stage** | A named group of jobs that run together | `stages:` list |
| **Job** | One unit of work with a script | A top-level key in `.gitlab-ci.yml` |
| **Runner** | The machine or container that executes a job | Registered separately, outside the file |

Read downward: a push creates a **pipeline**, the pipeline contains **stages** in order, each stage contains **jobs** that run in parallel, and each job is handed to a **runner** that actually runs the script.

The layer people forget is the runner. GitLab itself never executes anything. It decides what should run and hands it off. That is why a pipeline with no available runner sits pending forever with no error: nothing is wrong with your configuration, there is simply nobody to do the work.

## The default flow

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build-app:
  stage: build
  script: npm run build

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script: npm test

lint:
  stage: test
  script: npm run lint

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh staging
```

That pipeline runs in three waves:

1. `build-app` runs alone.
2. `unit-tests` and `lint` run **at the same time**, because they share a stage.
3. `deploy-staging` runs.

Two rules produce that behaviour, and they are worth stating explicitly because everything else builds on them:

- **Jobs in the same stage run in parallel.**
- **A stage does not start until every job in the previous stage has succeeded.**

A job with no `stage:` key goes into `test` by default, which regularly puts jobs somewhere their author did not intend.

## Breaking the stage lockstep

Strict stage ordering is simple but wasteful. If `lint` takes 20 seconds and `unit-tests` takes 8 minutes, the deploy waits 8 minutes even though it only really depends on the build.

`needs:` replaces stage ordering with explicit dependencies, turning the pipeline into a directed acyclic graph:

```yaml
deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  needs: [build-app]        # start as soon as the build is done
  script: ./deploy.sh staging
```

The job now starts the moment `build-app` finishes, regardless of whether the test stage is still running. On pipelines with uneven job durations this is often the single largest speed-up available.

The trade-off is legibility, a DAG is harder to reason about than a column of stages, so it is worth applying where the saving is real rather than everywhere.

## Where artifacts and cache fit

Every job runs in a **fresh, isolated environment**. Nothing carries over between jobs by default: not files, not installed packages, not environment variables set with `export`. That isolation is what makes pipelines reproducible, and it is also why two separate mechanisms exist for moving data between jobs.

| | Artifacts | Cache |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Preserve job **output** | Reuse job **input** |
| Guaranteed present | Yes | No |
| Visible in the UI | Yes, downloadable | No |
| Scope | Within a pipeline, and afterwards | Across pipelines |
| Typical contents | Build output, test reports, deploy bundles | `node_modules`, pip cache, Maven repository |

The distinction that actually matters is **correctness versus speed**.

Artifacts are a guarantee. A job that declares an artifact will have it available to the jobs that need it, and you can download it weeks later from the pipeline page.

Cache is an optimisation with no guarantee. It may be missing on a new branch, stale from an older run, or absent because the job landed on a different runner. A pipeline must still produce a correct result with every cache empty, if it does not, something that should be an artifact is being treated as cache.

The practical test: **would the pipeline still be correct if this data vanished?** If yes, cache. If no, artifact.

Full detail in [Artifacts](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-artifacts) and [Cache](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-cache).

## What triggers a pipeline

Not all pipelines are the same kind, and several CI variables behave differently depending on which one is running. The most common source of rules that mysteriously never match.

| Type | Triggered by | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Branch pipeline | A push to a branch | `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is set |
| Merge request pipeline | Opening or updating a merge request | `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is **not** set |
| Scheduled pipeline | A cron schedule in the UI | Good for nightly integration suites |
| Tag pipeline | Pushing a tag | The usual release trigger |
| Child pipeline | A `trigger:` job in the same project | Splits large configurations |
| Multi-project pipeline | A `trigger:` job naming another project | Coordinates across repositories |

A rule written as `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"` will never match inside a merge request pipeline, because that variable is not populated there. This catches almost everyone once.

## Controlling the pipeline as a whole

Individual jobs are filtered with `rules:`. The pipeline itself is governed by a top-level `workflow:` block:

```yaml
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH
```

That block is worth understanding because it solves the most common annoyance in GitLab CI: **duplicate pipelines**. Without it, a push to a branch with an open merge request creates both a branch pipeline and a merge request pipeline, doubling your runner minutes and cluttering the UI. The third rule suppresses the branch pipeline when a merge request already exists.

Defining this once at the top is much better than repeating the same conditions on every job.

## Where to go next

| Topic | What you will learn |
|---|---|
| [Stages and Jobs](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-stages-jobs) | Full syntax, job keywords, `rules`, parallel jobs and `needs` |
| [Artifacts](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-artifacts) | Passing files between jobs, report types, expiry |
| [Cache](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-cache) | Cache keys, policies, fallbacks and invalidation |
| [Pipeline Rules](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-ci-pipeline-rules) | Controlling exactly when jobs and pipelines run |
| [Runners](/tutorials/cicd/gitlab-runners) | Executors, registration, tags and concurrency |

---

## Final Takeaway

A GitLab pipeline is four layers: an event creates a **pipeline**, which contains ordered **stages**, which contain parallel **jobs**, each executed by a **runner**. Jobs are isolated from one another, so **artifacts** move guaranteed output forward and **cache** speeds up repeated inputs without any guarantee. `workflow:` decides whether a pipeline runs at all; `rules:` decides which jobs are in it; `needs:` lets you escape strict stage ordering when it costs too much time.

Get those relationships straight and the syntax in the detailed guides is mostly bookkeeping.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a pipeline, a stage and a job?**

A job is a single unit of work with its own script, running in its own isolated environment on a runner. A stage is a named group of jobs that execute in parallel with each other. A pipeline is one complete run of all the stages, triggered by an event such as a push, a merge request, a tag or a schedule. Stages run in sequence and, by default, each waits for every job in the previous stage to succeed before starting.

**Do jobs in the same stage run at the same time?**

Yes, provided runners are available to take them. That is the defining property of a stage. Putting two jobs in `test` means they run concurrently, and the stage is complete only when both finish. If jobs in a stage appear to run one after another, you have fewer free runners than jobs, or the runner's `concurrent` setting limits how many it will execute simultaneously.

**What is the difference between artifacts and cache?**

Artifacts preserve a job's output and are guaranteed to reach the jobs that need them, as well as being downloadable from the GitLab UI. Cache stores reusable inputs such as `node_modules` to make later runs faster, with no guarantee it will be there. It can be missing on a new branch, stale, or absent because the job ran on a different runner. The test is whether the pipeline would still be correct if the data vanished: if yes, cache; if no, artifacts.

**Why are two pipelines created every time I push?**

Because both branch pipelines and merge request pipelines are running for the same commit. When a branch has an open merge request, GitLab creates a pipeline for the branch and another for the merge request unless you tell it otherwise. The standard fix is a top-level `workflow: rules:` block that runs the merge request pipeline when one exists, suppresses the branch pipeline in that case, and always runs on the default branch. Defining it once at the top applies it to the whole pipeline.

**Why doesn't my rule match on merge requests?**

Because `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is not set in a merge request pipeline. It only exists in branch pipelines, so a condition written against it silently never matches when the pipeline was triggered by a merge request event. Use `$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME` for the branch name in that context, or branch on `$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"` to distinguish the pipeline type explicitly.

**Can a job start before the previous stage finishes?**

Yes, with `needs:`. Listing the specific jobs a job depends on lets it begin as soon as those have completed, ignoring stage boundaries and turning the pipeline into a directed acyclic graph. This can cut total runtime substantially when job durations are uneven. A deploy that only needs the build no longer waits for a slow test suite. The cost is that the pipeline becomes harder to read, so it is worth using where the time saving is genuine rather than applying it everywhere.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between artifacts and cache in GitLab CI?

Artifacts preserve job output that matters to the result, compiled binaries, test reports, deployment bundles, and are passed to later jobs and downloadable from the UI. Cache stores reusable inputs such as node_modules or a pip download directory to make future runs faster. The distinction that matters is correctness: artifacts are guaranteed to be there, while a cache may be missing, stale or from another branch, so a pipeline must never depend on cache contents to produce a correct result.
How do I pass files from one job to another?

Declare them as artifacts in the producing job with artifacts: paths:, and by default every job in a later stage downloads them automatically. To control that precisely, use needs: to name the specific jobs whose artifacts you want, or dependencies: to restrict it, dependencies: [] downloads nothing at all, which is worth setting on jobs that do not need them since it speeds them up noticeably.
How long are artifacts kept?

Until their expire_in elapses, defaulting to 30 days on GitLab.com unless the instance or project overrides it. Set expire_in explicitly on every artifact: an hour is plenty for files only passed between jobs in the same pipeline, while release builds might justify weeks. Artifacts consume project storage and are a common cause of unexpectedly hitting a storage quota, since a pipeline running dozens of times a day accumulates quickly. The latest artifacts for the most recent successful pipeline on a ref are kept regardless unless you disable that behaviour.
What is artifacts: reports: for?

It tells GitLab that an artifact is a structured report of a known type, JUnit test results, code coverage, SAST findings, a dotenv file, so the platform can parse it and surface the contents in the merge request rather than leaving it as a file to download. A JUnit report turns into a test summary showing exactly which tests newly failed, which is far more useful than reading a log. Report artifacts are subject to their own retention rules and, for some types, size limits.
Why are my artifacts empty or missing?

Usually the paths are wrong relative to the project root, which is where they are evaluated from, not from wherever the script happened to cd. The job log lists which files were collected, so check there first. The other frequent cause is that the job failed before producing them: by default artifacts are only uploaded when a job succeeds, so if you want them from failures too, for example to capture logs or screenshots, set artifacts: when: always.
Can I download artifacts without using the UI?

Yes. The GitLab API exposes them at a per-job endpoint, and there is a stable URL for the latest artifacts from a successful job on a given ref, which is what most external tooling uses. A CI job token authorises access from within another pipeline, which is how multi-project pipelines consume builds from an upstream project without a personal access token.
